sentences: We argue that this is the core conceptual issue: sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as blindly choosing the largest values from a bag of entries.
Based on this view, we propose Matrix Approximation Sparse Attention (MASA).
MASA replaces raw attention-mass ranking with a closed-form score that measures how much each sparse unit reduces matrix-product approximation error.
As a theory-grounded plug-in correction, MASA can be added to existing sparse attention frameworks without changing their sparse kernels or budgets.

Extensive experiments across multiple sparse attention methods, benchmarks, and LLM backbones show consistent accuracy gains, supporting both MASA and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention.

MASA improves all eight matched average scores across three sparse methods, three benchmark suites, and both Llama- and Qwen-family backbones.
MASA nevertheless delivers substantial gains relative to the dense-reference differences in several settings.
On InfiniteBench, MASA raises FlexPrefill-Llama from 47.14 to 47.99 against a full-attention score of 48.06, recovering approximately 92% of the original average-score deficit.
On RULER, MASA raises SeerAttention from 87.60 to 88.09, moving it from below the dense reference to above it.
For FlexPrefill-Llama on RULER, replacing the ranking score adds 0.76 points, exceeding the original method’s 0.48-point advantage over full attention and increasing that advantage to 1.24 points.
Thus, MASA improves already strong sparse systems without increasing their sparse budgets or changing their kernels.

Across the four RULER configurations at 32K, 64K, and 128K, MASA improves 11 of 12 matched length-level scores.
For every configuration, the mean gain over these longer contexts at 32K–128K exceeds that at 4K–16K.
At 128K, MASA improves MInference, SeerAttention, FlexPrefill-Llama, and FlexPrefill-Qwen by 1.28, 0.48, 1.45, and 2.16 points, respectively.
At 64K, the gains reach 2.16 points for FlexPrefill-Llama and 3.65 points for FlexPrefill-Qwen.
On LongBench, MASA improves SeerAttention’s 8K+ score from 52.69 to 53.16.
These results support the value of matrix-approximation ranking for long-context sparse prefill under the original frameworks’ sparse budgets and kernels.
The evaluated MASA configurations reduce normalized squared output error in all four framework–backbone pairs, providing direct empirical support for matrix-product preservation.

Across MInference, SeerAttention, FlexPrefill-Llama, and FlexPrefill-Qwen, replacing the original ranking score with MASA adds empirically negligible overhead relative to the sparse attention runtime and remains far below the dense attention cost.
The overhead also stays negligible at 128K, the main regime where sparse attention is needed.
Therefore, MASA improves accuracy without weakening the practical efficiency of the underlying sparse attention method.
